name: The Streisand Effect
statement: Trying to suppress information is often what makes it spread.
statementAccent: is often what makes it spread
meaning: The act of censoring something is itself newsworthy. The takedown notice tells everyone there is something worth looking at, and hands them the reason to look.
mechanism: Attention is the scarce resource, and an attempt to suppress information advertises that the information is worth suppressing. The act of censorship is itself newsworthy, it signals value, and online it provokes copying faster than any one party can delete. The effort to shrink the audience is what enlarges it.

examples.text: In 2003 Barbra Streisand sued a photographer over an aerial shot of her Malibu home — one frame in a 12,000-image coastal-erosion survey. Before the suit the photo had been downloaded six times, two of them by her own lawyers; news of the lawsuit brought more than 420,000 visitors to the site within a month. The case was dismissed and she was ordered to pay the photographer's legal costs. (The download and visitor figures are the widely-cited ones, sourced to the project itself.)

In 2007 the licensing body behind HD DVD sent takedown notices over a leaked 16-byte decryption key, and the site Digg began deleting posts that carried it. The deletions triggered a user revolt: within days the key appeared on hundreds of thousands of pages — far more than would ever have noticed it otherwise.

In 2009 the oil trader Trafigura obtained a UK 'super-injunction' so sweeping it barred The Guardian from even reporting that an injunction existed. When it appeared to block reporting of a question in Parliament, outrage on Twitter spread the suppressed report far and wide, and the gag was swiftly varied.

whyItMatters: Before sending the lawyer's letter, ask how many people have actually seen the thing and how many will see it once the letter becomes the story. Suppression is only worth attempting where it can be complete and quiet; otherwise it is advertising you pay for twice.

working.lead: Count who has actually seen it
working.text: if the audience is currently tiny, a visible takedown may be the first thing that gives it a large one.

working.lead: Suppress only where you can be complete and quiet
working.text: removal works when it is total and unremarkable; a partial, contested takedown just advertises the target.

working.lead: Don't let the takedown become the story
working.text: heavy-handed legal threats are themselves newsworthy — weigh the coverage of the suppression against the coverage of the thing.
a correction, a right-of-reply, or silence often shrinks attention where a lawsuit would multiply it.

limits: The effect is not a rule that suppression always backfires — it names the specific case where the attempt itself becomes the story. The cases we remember (Streisand, the AACS key, Trafigura) are memorable precisely because they went viral; the vast majority of takedown notices, cease-and-desists, and quiet removals succeed unremarkably and are never noticed, so the effect suffers heavy survivorship bias. It is also not an argument against enforcing genuine rights — defamation, privacy, and copyright remedies still work in ordinary cases. Virality needs an interested audience, a sympathetic framing, and the network to carry it; absent those, suppression tends to simply work.
misreadings: It does not mean suppression always backfires — plenty of takedowns succeed quietly; it names the specific case where the attempt itself becomes the story. Nor is it an argument that nothing should ever be removed. It is a warning that visible, aggressive suppression can be the loudest possible amplifier.
origin: Mike Masnick coined the term on Techdirt on 5 January 2005, writing about a Florida resort's attempt to force the photo-sharing site urinal.net to remove a picture of its urinal: "Let's call it the Streisand Effect." He named it for Streisand's failed 2003 suit over the aerial photograph of her house. (The sum she sued for is usually given as US$50 million, though contemporary reports varied.)
